n0001.title: Towards a Theory of Bugs
n0001.gist: Because simple programs can already be as computationally sophisticated as any system, bugs are an unavoidable sign of real computation, not mere human error.
n0001.question: Bugs in software — can there be a general scientific theory of why programs misbehave? (an argument from computation itself)

n0002.title: "My Program Did the Wrong Thing!"
n0002.gist: Bugs arise because simple mental models of a program can fail to match its actual, computationally sophisticated behavior, a gap rooted in computational irreducibility.
n0002.question: Bugs — why do simple programs produce unexpected results? (a conceptual framework)

n0007.title: "My Program Did the Wrong Thing!"
n0007.gist: Programs misbehave because even simple-looking code can carry out computation too sophisticated for our simple mental models to foresee, a phenomenon rooted in computational irreducibility.

n0015.title: Bugs in Turing Machines
n0015.gist: Testing simple Turing machines meant to compute n+1 shows that even tiny, well-behaved-looking programs eventually produce glitches at larger inputs, and the point where this first happens varies unpredictably.
n0015.question: Turing machines — how far must you test before a hidden bug shows up? (worked examples)

n0016.title: A simple machine's hidden glitch
n0016.gist: A basic 3-state Turing machine appears to compute n+1 correctly for small inputs, but at n=7 it suddenly outputs 9 instead of 8, revealing an unexpected flaw.

n0025.title: Pattern of the glitches
n0025.gist: The errors recur at inputs whose binary form ends in 111, because the machine's head performs extra unnecessary moves that scribble wrong digits onto the tape in those cases.

n0030.title: How soon do bugs appear
n0030.gist: Among thousands of small Turing machines that seem to compute n+1 correctly, some hide their first error until much larger inputs, with the most insidious bug delayed until n=15.

n0044.title: Larger machines, later bugs
n0044.gist: Among millions of 4-state Turing machines that successfully compute n+1 for small inputs, some conceal bugs that only appear at much larger values, here first failing at n=63.

n0052.title: What Counts as a Bug?
n0052.gist: Calling something a bug requires a precise specification of intended behavior, and different kinds of specifications—equivalence, restriction, or property—all turn out to have hidden counterexamples.
n0052.question: Bugs — what kind of specification lets us say a program has one? (several specification types examined)

n0053.title: Specifications define bugs
n0053.gist: A program always does exactly what it does, so calling something a bug requires comparing it against some separate, more easily grasped specification of intended behavior.

n0057.title: Equivalence as specification
n0057.gist: One way to define a bug is requiring two differently written versions of a program to behave identically, yet two Turing machines that seem to match diverge unpredictably at input 27.

n0064.title: Negative constraints on behavior
n0064.gist: Specifications can instead forbid certain behaviors, like unbounded memory use or infinite looping, yet machines that seem well behaved for many steps can suddenly violate these constraints anyway.

n0075.title: A parity constraint fails too
n0075.gist: Even a simple constraint like requiring only even outputs can seem satisfied for many inputs before a machine suddenly breaks it, here producing an odd number at n=32.

n0081.title: A Cellular Automaton Example
n0081.gist: Cellular automata built to double an input size often work correctly for a long stretch of inputs before developing a bug, and simple visual inspection can sometimes—but not always—guarantee correctness.
n0081.question: Cellular automata — can you tell just by looking whether a rule will always work correctly? (several worked cases)

n0082.title: Doubling cellular automata
n0082.gist: Cellular automata can be designed to double the size of an input pattern, and many different rules accomplish this task with varying efficiency and complexity.

n0088.title: Bugs appear after delay
n0088.gist: Some doubling rules that look correct for many inputs suddenly fail at a later input, with the first failure sometimes delayed to input sizes like 24 or 32 before showing up.

n0097.title: Visual obviousness versus uncertainty
n0097.gist: Some cellular automaton patterns are visually simple enough to guarantee no bugs exist, but others that look similarly contained show irregular fluctuations whose long-term safety is not obvious from inspection alone.

n0110.title: Testing containment further
n0110.gist: A second seemingly contained pattern also shows random-looking fluctuations in how long it takes to settle, again leaving open whether it might eventually leak and produce a bug.

n0118.title: Proving no bugs exist
n0118.gist: By analyzing the whole computational process rather than just overall statistics, one can show a boundary region always moves inward and the pattern behind it can never die out, proving the cellular automaton always correctly doubles its input.

n0133.title: But What about Formal Proofs?
n0133.gist: A Turing machine's correct behavior can sometimes be formally proved using symbolic representations and induction, but for machines with real bugs no such proof exists because the claim is false.
n0133.question: Formal proofs — can symbolic logic settle whether a program is bug-free? (a worked proof and its failure case)

n0134.title: Representing machines symbolically
n0134.gist: To prove a Turing machine's behavior, its tape and head position are encoded as symbolic linked-list expressions, with axioms describing how the machine's rules transform this symbolic representation step by step.

n0159.title: Proving correctness by induction
n0159.gist: Using these symbolic axioms, one can mechanically derive a finite inductive proof that a given Turing machine always correctly computes n+1 for every possible input, reducing an infinite claim to a finite argument.

n0181.title: Searching the proof graph
n0181.gist: Proofs correspond to paths through a multiway graph of derivable theorems built from the axioms, and for a genuinely buggy machine no such path to the false claim can ever be found, however far one searches.

n0184.title: Computational Irreducibility and the Limits of Testing
n0184.gist: Because computational irreducibility is ubiquitous, no finite amount of testing, sampling, or accumulated facts can guarantee a program free of surprising bugs, however rare they may be.
n0184.question: Computational irreducibility — why can't testing or induction ever fully rule out hidden bugs? (several supporting arguments)

n0185.title: Irreducibility as the source of bugs
n0185.gist: Because the Principle of Computational Equivalence makes sophisticated, unpredictable computation common even in simple systems, no bounded amount of reasoning can rule out a program eventually surprising us with a bug.

n0196.title: Induction fails in ruliology
n0196.gist: Observing a pattern across many tested cases cannot guarantee it continues forever, because computational irreducibility means ruliological systems can always violate a law inferred from limited evidence.

n0203.title: Sampling and bug density
n0203.gist: Whether random testing finds a bug depends on how computationally strong the randomness is relative to the program and how rare the bugs are, which in principle can be made arbitrarily small, like a busy-beaver problem.

n0209.title: Some Typical Ruliological Surprises
n0209.gist: Across cellular automata, Turing machines, combinators, and growth processes, simple rules repeatedly produce behavior far more complex or sudden than their simplicity would suggest, confirming surprises are the norm.
n0209.question: Ruliological surprises — how often does simple exploration of rules turn up unexpected complexity? (a gallery of examples)

n0210.title: Early surprises in simple rules
n0210.gist: Among simple cellular automata, almost all enumerated rules behaved predictably until rule 30 appeared, producing unexpectedly intricate and complex patterns, a similarly delayed surprise occurring later for Turing machines.

n0217.title: Input-dependent surprises
n0217.gist: A cellular automaton rule that behaves simply for most starting inputs can suddenly produce a qualitatively different, ever-growing, or wholly unforeseeable pattern once the input reaches some particular larger value.

n0226.title: Halting and growth surprises
n0226.gist: Processes like combinator evaluation, two-dimensional cellular automata, and constrained multiway growth can appear to continue predictably for very long stretches before abruptly halting, losing symmetry, or getting permanently stuck.

n0244.title: Mathematical "Bugs"
n0244.gist: Mathematical patterns found from many examples can fail at astronomically large counterexamples, but mainstream mathematics mostly avoids such bugs because it focuses on human-graspable, reducible structures.
n0244.question: Mathematics — can mathematical patterns also harbor hidden counterexamples like software bugs? (two numerical examples)

n0245.title: Counterexamples found far out
n0245.gist: Patterns in polynomial factor coefficients and in prime-counting differences hold for enormous numbers of tested cases before eventually failing, at x^105−1 and at the 23,338,590,792nd prime respectively.

n0256.title: Why mathematics mostly avoids bugs
n0256.gist: Pure mathematics largely sidesteps computational irreducibility because it deliberately concentrates on human-level questions within pockets of reducibility, while experimental mathematics, like ruliology, remains exposed to genuine surprises.

n0261.title: Bugs in Practice
n0261.gist: Avoiding bugs in practice depends on well-designed language primitives and on visualizing a program's inner workings, though any program doing real computation—including trained neural networks—remains exposed to unforeseeable behavior.
n0261.question: Bugs in practice — what can programmers actually do to limit, understand, or live with them? (several practical strategies)

n0262.title: Language design limits bugs
n0262.gist: Because fully understanding a program's every behavior would make running it pointless, the best practical defense is a well-designed language whose primitives match human intent, reducing the chance of unwanted surprises.

n0272.title: Seeing inside a program
n0272.gist: Visualizing a program's internal computation, as with cellular automaton spacetime patterns, gives practical confidence about correctness that formal proof from description alone would find immeasurably harder to establish.

n0275.title: AI, neural nets and unpredictability
n0275.gist: Modern AI can catch familiar human-style coding mistakes, but deeper bugs arising from computation's own nature also afflict trained neural networks, whose irreducible internal workings remain essentially impossible to fully understand or guarantee.

n0280.title: Allowing bugs, learning from them
n0280.gist: Allowing some bugs can shorten low-level programs by trading exactness for raw computational economy, and what looks like failure in engineering can instead count as scientific discovery about computation's hidden richness.

n0283.title: Thanks
n0283.gist: Acknowledgements to colleagues and the Wolfram quality assurance team who helped shape the author's understanding of bugs.
